title: Building a word-driven decision
idea: Turn a 'react to this word' problem into code. Learner picks the comparison and arranges a small handler, then predicts results.

exercises.prompt: Task: a traffic light word decides an action. "red" -> "Stop", "yellow" -> "Slow", "green" -> "Go", anything else -> "Broken light". The output is...
options: one of four messages depending on the word
exercises.explanation: Four possible messages, chosen by which word came in. Naming the outputs tells you the branch count.

exercises.prompt: What single INPUT drives the decision?
exercises.explanation: One word comes in - the light color - and one action goes out. Simple word-to-action mapping.
One branch per known color, else as the catch-all for anything unexpected.
== compares the word in light against the literal "red".
"yellow" fails the red test, matches the yellow elif, so "Slow" prints.
"purple" matches no known color, so the else catches it: "Broken light".

exercises.prompt: Why is the catch-all else a good habit for word handlers?
options: Real input can be anything, so you always want a response for the unexpected
exercises.explanation: Words you did not plan for will show up. The else keeps the program graceful instead of silent.

options: Broken light - because "Red" does not equal "red"
exercises.explanation: Case matters: "Red" is not "red", so no color branch matches and the else runs. A real capitalization gotcha.

exercises.prompt: Checking the hand examples ("red", "yellow", "green", and an odd word) proves all four branches work.
exercises.explanation: Yes - one test per branch, including an unexpected word for the else, confirms the whole handler.

exercises.prompt: Good first step for a 'react to this word' task?
options: List the known words and their actions, then write one branch each plus an else
exercises.explanation: Mapping each word to its action first gives you the branch structure directly - then the code writes itself.
